value.overview: The American Pipit is a slender, ground-feeding songbird of open country. It breeds mainly in Arctic and subarctic tundra and in alpine areas of western North America, then moves south for winter. Its plain gray-brown appearance, thin bill, long legs, constantly moving gait, and white-edged tail help distinguish it from sparrows. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon visitor, with records treated as accidental or very rare rather than as a regular wintering species.
value.classification: The American Pipit belongs to the pipit and wagtail family Motacillidae. It is one of several closely related North American pipits and was formerly included in the broader Buff-bellied Pipit complex.
value.identification: A medium-small, slim songbird measuring about 15–18 cm, the American Pipit is usually grayish brown above with a pale, finely streaked underside. It has a narrow pointed bill, long dark legs, a relatively long tail, and pale or white outer tail feathers visible in flight. Breeding adults can show warmer or cleaner underparts, while winter birds are more heavily streaked. It walks with a characteristic tail bob and often flies with fluttering, undulating movements.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across Arctic and subarctic North America and in alpine habitats of the western mountains. During migration and winter it occupies open, sparsely vegetated ground, including shorelines, mudflats, agricultural fields, short grasslands, barren areas, and high-elevation meadows. In Costa Rica, the American Pipit is not a regular resident; it has been recorded only rarely, generally as an accidental or highly unusual migrant or winter visitor. Any Costa Rican record should be documented carefully because of its scarcity there.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Most individuals move south from northern breeding grounds in autumn and return in spring. In Costa Rica it is accidental or very rare, with no reliable evidence of a regular seasonal population.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs in open tundra, alpine meadows, rocky slopes, and other treeless northern habitats. The female usually places a cup-shaped nest on or near the ground, often concealed among grass, moss, or low vegetation. The clutch commonly contains several eggs, and both adults participate in feeding the young. The species generally raises one or more broods during the short northern summer, when abundant insects are available.
value.dietFeeding: The American Pipit feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, including beetles, flies, caterpillars, grasshoppers, and aquatic larvae. Seeds and other plant material may become more important outside the breeding season. It forages by walking steadily across open ground, pausing to pick prey from soil, vegetation, wet margins, or shallow water. It may gather in loose flocks where food is concentrated.
value.behavior: This active pipit spends much of its time on the ground and frequently bobs or wags its tail while walking. It is usually alert and may flush suddenly into a low, undulating flight, showing pale outer tail feathers. Migrating birds can travel in flocks and give sharp, high-pitched call notes overhead. Males sing from the ground, a perch, or during flight, especially on the breeding grounds.

conservation.populationTrend: Despite its broad range and global Least Concern status, the species has experienced a substantial long-term decline in parts of North America, including a marked reduction in estimated nonbreeding abundance in recent monitoring. The magnitude and causes of trends in Central America, including Costa Rica, are poorly documented.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include loss and degradation of open wetland, shoreline, grassland, and agricultural habitats used during migration and winter. Climate change may alter Arctic and alpine breeding habitats, seasonal food availability, and migration conditions. Pesticide use and disturbance of heavily used open areas may also reduce local feeding opportunities.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore open wetlands, shorelines, grasslands, and other nonforested habitats used by migrating and wintering pipits. Reduce unnecessary pesticide use, protect high-elevation and Arctic breeding environments, and maintain careful bird-monitoring programs. In Costa Rica, reporting unusual sightings with photographs, sound recordings, date, and precise location can improve knowledge of this rare visitor.
